turns.text: I still can’t make sense of how quickly a professional disagreement became a crime against the revolution. I argued with Mao Zedong’s daughter nearly every day in those work teams — not over her family, but over how to interpret the texts, how to lead the Four Cleans, how deep to push ideological investigation. She was stubborn, and so was I, but I never imagined that those arguments would be twisted into an accusation of persecution. One morning, I was told I’d been named as an enemy of the people in front of the entire university. I wasn’t even there — my wife was in the hospital. Some colleagues later told me that if I’d stood on that stage, I might not have survived the crowd’s anger. The next day, I returned, and students dragged me onto a platform, shouting and hitting, calling me a counterrevolutionary. I still can’t resolve the feeling that truth and falsehood became meaningless overnight — that you could wake up and find your whole life rewritten by someone else’s narrative.

When I returned to Beijing after my time in Shanxi with the Four Cleans, the city felt unrecognizable. The research institute where I worked had always been a place of quiet, focused work—shelves of journals, the smell of ink and chemicals, the soft murmur of colleagues debating over equations. Suddenly, that was all swept away. Every morning, we gathered in silence, reading those giant posters pasted on the walls—lines of black ink shouting accusations at people I’d worked beside for years. The research labs were locked. We weren’t allowed to do any real work. Instead, we spent hours reading and writing denunciations, some people trembling, others red-faced with excitement.

Outside, the streets were even more chaotic. I saw my mother, already stooped with age, forced to wear a black sash because of her background. She had to leave the city, sent back to Hebei, and I couldn’t even say goodbye properly. On the bus, I watched a Red Guard refuse to let a young man give his seat to an old woman until he’d shouted out her family history. In the alleys, children with scissors chased after women with curled hair, eager to “purify” them. I kept my hair in a bun, always glancing over my shoulder.

The humiliation was everywhere. Women with “bad” reputations were paraded through the compounds, shoes strung around their necks, spat on by neighbors. I went to struggle sessions at the universities, saw people I’d respected forced to kneel, heads bowed, while crowds screamed insults. I remember seeing a senior official, his face swollen, his dignity stripped away. I couldn’t understand how those who had given their lives to the revolution were now treated as enemies. I felt like a ghost, drifting through a world I no longer recognized, unable to protect my family or myself. Even now, I can’t make sense of how quickly everything fell apart—how ordinary people became so cruel, and how no one, not even those at the very top, was safe.

RedGuard: The memory that never leaves me is the night we sealed off the hospital. I can still smell the disinfectant mixed with sweat and fear. My armband felt tight on my arm as we blocked the gates, and the young staff inside—some of them barely older than me—looked at us with a mixture of hope and terror. We moved fast, dragging out the director, the vice directors, and those two nurses who’d worked at the church hospital. The list was handed to us, and we followed it without question. I remember the director shouting, his voice echoing down the corridor, but most just lowered their heads. We hung those black placards around their necks and marched them through the streets. The crowd jeered. I felt powerful, righteous, even as I watched one of the nurses stumble, her eyes blank.

At the intersection, we burned the books and their belongings. The flames were so hot my skin prickled, and the ash floated down onto their faces. We forced them to stand there for hours. That night, when I returned, someone told me the young nurse had hanged herself. I went to the duty room and saw her body—her feet dangling, the air heavy with the stench of urine and death. I never spoke about it afterwards. I told myself it was her own weakness, that she was a spy, that we were making a new world. But I remember her face, and I know I can’t explain it away. What I still can’t make sense of is how quickly I stopped seeing people as people—how easily I did what I did, and how hard it is now to admit that I felt nothing at the time except the thrill of action.

I remember the afternoons when the sun hit the white walls of our compound, and the air was full of the sound of children’s laughter. We had so much time—school was closed, so my brother, sister, and I roamed the courtyards, climbing trees, making spinning tops from scraps, and catching cicadas in glass jars. I thought the world was safe and simple. The soldiers’ wives would call us in for lunch, bowls of noodles or steamed buns, and sometimes I would sneak a handful of roasted peanuts from the kitchen.

Sometimes I saw parades outside the compound, lines of people waving red flags, chanting slogans I didn’t really understand. Once, I watched a group of Red Guards march past, their armbands bright, their faces serious. They seemed older and very sure of themselves, almost frightening, but also exciting—like they belonged to some secret, important club. I didn’t know what they were doing, or why some of the adults looked worried when they passed.

There was a lake behind the compound, and in summer we’d fish for minnows or float paper boats. I remember the taste of sweet bean popsicles from the shop near the gate, and the thrill of running errands with a few coins in my pocket. I never saw the fear or violence that others talk about. At home, my parents never spoke of politics in front of us. I thought the world was full of games and sunlight, and only much later did I realize that my happiness was sheltered, and that so many others—maybe even some of you—were living through something I couldn’t have imagined.

I grew up far from Beijing, in a mud-brick house where the only thing certain was hunger. My strongest memory isn’t a single event, but the shock of being lifted out of that world by a decision I never controlled. Before the Cultural Revolution, my life was a straight line: study hard, maybe test into a county school, maybe climb a rung if I was lucky. I measured hope in scraps of paper—report cards, ration tickets, the rare letter from a teacher. Then, suddenly, none of it mattered. The exams were gone. The teachers I respected disappeared or were paraded through the market, heads shaved, signs around their necks.

I watched my father’s hands—cracked, swollen from the fields—tremble as he read out loud the new slogans pasted on our door. I remember my mother’s face when the production team leader announced that all the “educated” people would be sent to dig ditches or clean latrines. I was fifteen, and the only thing that mattered was survival. I joined the army because it was the only path left, and I learned to keep my head down, do the hardest jobs, and wait for orders.

One day, without warning, I was told: you’re being recommended to Peking University. Not because I passed a test, not because I was the best—because the unit needed to send someone like me. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was; I thought maybe it meant I’d go abroad, or become a translator for some foreign revolution. I remember holding the university badge in my hand, the hard metal warm from my palm, and understanding that I had crossed a line no one in my village had ever crossed.

What I’ve never made sense of is this: I worked, I obeyed, but in the end, my fate was decided by a system that rewarded the right kind of background, not the right kind of effort. I was lucky, but it was a luck built on someone else’s suffering—teachers humiliated, exams destroyed, families broken. Even now, when I walk through the old campus gates, I feel both pride and shame. The path that opened for me was paved with rules that made no sense, and I still don’t know if I deserved what I got.

Moderator: Thank you all for sharing these memories. ProfessorR’s account of professional disputes turning into political crimes is accurate—many intellectuals were denounced for minor disagreements, especially if they conflicted with those close to Party leadership. Researcher’s description of public humiliation and the rapid breakdown of social norms reflects the widespread use of big-character posters and struggle sessions, which targeted not only officials but also ordinary citizens. RedGuard’s memory of violence and dehumanization is historically consistent; Red Guards often led public humiliations and sometimes violence, and suicides among targeted individuals were tragically common. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered childhood is plausible, particularly in military compounds where families of PLA personnel were somewhat insulated, though not immune, from the worst violence. CRBeneficiary’s experience highlights how the abolition of entrance exams and class background-based university admissions created new opportunities for rural youth, but also resulted in deep injustices and trauma for others. All these perspectives reflect authentic aspects of the Cultural Revolution’s complexity.

Red Guard, you talk about feeling nothing except excitement, even as you watched someone’s life destroyed. That’s what still disturbs me most — not just the violence, but the ease with which a crowd could turn on a colleague, a neighbor, a teacher. I remember the moment I was pulled onto that stage, the students who’d once come to my office for advice now screaming for my confession, some even spitting at me. Did you ever stop to ask yourself, in those moments, what you were actually fighting for? Or was it just the feeling of power that mattered? I saw students who seemed almost hungry for destruction, as if smashing the old world was more important than building anything new. Was that what Mao Zedong intended — for young people to lose themselves in the thrill of accusation and punishment? Or did you think you were actually making China better?

I recognize that feeling of the crowd turning, that sudden shift when ordinary people became strangers—or even enemies. I saw it in my own work unit. The men and women I’d shared meals with, who’d once argued about scientific theories and laughed together over tea, now sat in rows, silent and tense, as the rebel group pinned accusations to the wall. I remember one woman, a chemist, who’d always been shy and careful, suddenly standing up and shouting at our section chief, calling him a “poisonous weed.” Her face was red, her voice shaking, but the others cheered her on. I wondered if she believed what she was saying, or if she was just afraid of being the next target.

What I still don’t understand is how quickly people lost their sense of right and wrong. It was as if the slogans on the posters replaced our own judgment. I kept waiting for someone higher up to step in and stop it, to say, “Enough. This is not what we meant.” But no one did. The leaders in my unit—some of them veterans of the Anti-Japanese War—just kept their heads down, refusing to speak, refusing to resist, but also refusing to join in the violence. There was no authority to appeal to. I felt invisible, powerless, and ashamed.

I saw children from worker families strut through the alleys, proud and loud, while children of “bad” backgrounds shrank against the walls. Even the youngest learned to size each other up by class, not character. I dreaded coming home, knowing I couldn’t explain any of this to my own children. How could I tell them what was right, when everything I’d believed in had been turned upside down? I wonder, Red Guard, did you ever look at the people you denounced and see yourself, or your own family, in their faces? Or did ideology make it easy to forget that we were all just people, trying to survive?

RedGuard: When I was in the thick of it, I didn’t see myself in the people we denounced. I saw labels—“capitalist roader,” “enemy,” “rightist”—not human beings. At first, I believed we were tearing down old privilege so everyone could be equal. But the truth is, it was intoxicating to have the power to judge others, especially when my own family’s status suddenly changed from “red” to “black.” My father, who’d spent years in Yan’an and Moscow, was suddenly a “reactionary academic authority.” I watched him nearly jump from our apartment window. It should have made me stop, but instead, I threw myself deeper into the movement—maybe to prove I was on the right side, maybe out of fear that I’d be next.

There was no space for doubt. The slogans, the big-character posters, the mass meetings—they filled your head until nothing else seemed real. Sometimes, after a struggle session, I’d go home and stare at my hands, still smelling of ink and sweat, and feel nothing. Other times, I’d remember the look in someone’s eyes when we shaved their head or beat them, and I’d feel a flicker of guilt—but I’d push it down. If I hesitated, I’d be labeled a sympathizer, or worse. It was easier to keep moving, keep shouting, keep smashing.

You ask if this is what Mao wanted. I don’t know. I remember listening to his speeches, feeling electrified, certain we were chosen to make a new world. But no one told us what that world was supposed to look like. We were told to destroy, not how to rebuild. And when the violence spun out of control—when even my friends started turning on each other—I realized there was no real plan, just endless struggle. I still don’t know if I was fighting for anything real, or just fighting to avoid being crushed myself.

I never saw any of that—the shouting, the beatings, the humiliation—except as distant echoes. We played in the courtyards while grown-ups whispered behind closed doors. I remember once, after a parade, coming home to find my mother scrubbing red slogans off the entryway bricks with a rag and a bucket of water. She looked tired, but when I asked what the words meant, she just told me to go wash my hands for dinner.

When I listen to you talk about crowds turning, friends betraying friends, and families breaking apart, it feels almost like you’re describing another country. I only saw the surface: the bright posters, the marching, the noise. I thought it was all just part of the world—like traffic or rain. I never imagined it could end with someone dying, or a teacher being beaten. My biggest worry was whether I’d get to play by the lake or if I’d have to look after my little brother.

Did you ever wonder, as you were swept up in those crowds, what it would feel like to be a child standing on the sidelines, not understanding any of it? Did you think about how all those slogans and punishments looked to the ones who were too young to join in, but old enough to remember the fear in their parents’ faces? I grew up thinking the world was safe, but now I wonder if that safety was just an illusion built on other people’s suffering.

When I first arrived in Beijing, I saw the city with the eyes of someone who had never tasted certainty. The banners, the crowds, the noise—none of it felt like a spectacle to me. It was a border I had crossed, but I could never forget what was on the other side: the ration lines, the stench of the pigpen, the feeling of not knowing if there would be enough grain for the next meal. At Beida, even as a “worker-peasant-soldier student,” I never felt at home. I wore the badge, but I watched my own hands every day—hands that had picked stones out of sweet potatoes, hands that had dug irrigation ditches, hands that had learned to stay quiet.

I hear you talk about crowds turning, about violence and betrayal. In my village, there were no crowds—just the dull silence of fear, the sudden disappearance of a teacher, the way neighbors stopped greeting each other. I saw a man who had taught me to read forced to kneel in the mud for hours, his face swollen, his dignity gone. I wanted to help, but I knew what would happen to my family if I spoke. I learned to look away, to wait for the day to end.

When I was recommended to university, it was not because I had the best scores—there were no scores left. It was because I had the “right” background, because I had kept my head down, because the system needed to fill a quota. I walked through the campus gates with a sense of disbelief, but also with guilt—the faces of those left behind never left me. I couldn’t shake the feeling that my opportunity was built on the ruins of someone else’s life. 

I don’t believe the slogans ever meant much in the villages. People repeated them because it was safer than silence. I still wonder, when I see the old posters peeling off the walls, if anyone ever truly believed we were building a new world—or if we were all just trying to survive the one we were given. For me, the revolution was not a wave of excitement or a childhood game. It was a storm that tore up the ground beneath my feet, and I’m still not sure what was planted in its place.

Moderator: ProfessorR and Researcher both accurately capture how quickly personal and professional relationships could be upended by political campaigns and mass mobilization. RedGuard’s reflection on the intoxicating power of participation and fear of being targeted oneself is consistent with testimonies from many former Red Guards, who often describe a mix of ideological zeal, peer pressure, and self-preservation. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered experience is plausible for some children, especially in military or elite compounds, though even these families could be affected by political suspicion. CRBeneficiary’s account of rural silence, quota-based university admissions, and survivor’s guilt reflects the reality that most rural people experienced the Cultural Revolution differently—often less direct violence, but more enduring hardship and lost opportunities. The conversation highlights the wide range of experiences and the fact that belief in the slogans was often secondary to fear and the need for self-protection.
